subject: SLA provisioning tiers, monthly remedy routing and latency carve-in request
messages:
From: Alice Moreno <alice@nimbussoft.com>
To: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Cc: Procurement Team <procurement@nimbussoft.com>
Date: 2027-05-18T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Initial SLA ask and latency carve-in for batch workloads

Hi Priyom / Laura,

Thanks for the demo last week — Nimbus team is excited about Redwood's serving performance. We're starting procurement discussions and need to validate a few SLA points before we move to legal/PO stage. High-level asks are below:

- Baseline uptime: we'd like to see 99.95% for hosted inference (multi-region supported).
- Monthly remedy: propose credits up to 15% of monthly invoice for major availability misses; smaller outages should pro-rate.
- Latency commitments: important for interactive traffic — target p95 < 200ms, p99 < 600ms.
- Batched inference: we run nightly high-throughput jobs; can you provide an exception carve-in for batch windows (tolerate higher tail latency and give alternate remedy)?
- Maintenance windows: we prefer a single quarterly maintenance window; any emergency maintenance carveouts should be defined.

Attaching a short doc with our typical traffic mix and procurement timeline (requested PO by end of May). Can you share Redwood's standard SLA template and any provisioned/dedicated differences?

Thanks,
Alice
Alice Moreno
Head of Platform Ops, NimbusSoft
alice@nimbussoft.com

Date: 2027-05-18T11:04:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Initial SLA ask and latency carve-in for batch workloads

Hi Alice — thanks for the clear summary and the traffic profile. Quick responses to each bullet, and I've attached our standard SLA template for reference: redwood_sla_template_v1.pdf.

- Baseline uptime: Redwood hosted standard is 99.9% for general-purpose endpoints. For Dedicated/reserved capacity we typically offer 99.92%. We can discuss a path to 99.95% tied to a committed reserved pool if you plan to move to Dedicated.
- Monthly remedy: our template uses a tiered credit table (0.5%–10% of monthly fees depending on slack). We can consider increasing the top-end for strategic customers under a commitment schedule, but we'd need to align on commit size and term.
- Latency: our interactive SLOs are typically p95 < 250ms / p99 < 750ms for single-request interactive models on dedicated capacity. Hosted can be subject to higher variance during burst.
- Batched inference: we do carve out batched windows for latency — those runs are treated under a different SLO profile and a separate remedy pool. We will need to scope the daily/weekly windows and expected QPS during those jobs.
- Maintenance: standard is monthly rolling maintenance with a 4-hour window; for Dedicated we can negotiate quarterly maintenance windows and notice periods.

Next steps: Laura, can your team review this template and propose redlines? Karthik, can you confirm the technical feasibility of tightening interactive p95/p99 for a committed Dedicated pool?

I'll hold a short call with Alice's team on Thursday if that works — to walk the table and discuss commit vs hosted trade-offs.

Best,
Priyom
Priyom Das
Senior Customer Success Manager, Redwood Inference
priyom_das@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Initial SLA ask and latency carve-in for batch workloads

Hi Alice / team — looping legal for redlines. I've reviewed Redwood's template and marked a few items in the attached PDF (SLA_redline_nimbus_v2.pdf):

- Uptime: propose a two-track approach in the contract body — Hosted baseline at 99.90% with a migration credit ladder and Dedicated baseline at 99.92. For a 12‑month committed Dedicated agreement we can add a one-time uplift to 99.95% (subject to minimum committed spend).
- Remedy caps: we'll push back on an uncapped 15% top-level credit. Industry-standard upper bound is capped (we recommend 10% or a capped dollar amount). Requesting a fixed cap preserves financial predictability.
- Latency SLOs: we can accept the interactive p95/p99 listed by Priyom on Dedicated, but batched windows must be explicitly defined and excluded from the interactive SLA. We recommend a clear definition clause (start/end times, expected batch QPS, and a sample timeframe for measuring tails).
- Maintenance carveouts: add required notification windows (7 days for scheduled; 24 hours for non-critical updates; immediate notification for emergency security patches).

Please see inline comments. Priyom — happy to jump on the call to walk the redlines. Alice — if you can confirm whether Nimbus can accept a capped remedy of 10% (or define an alternate cap), that helps speed approvals.

Thanks,
Laura Bennett
Director, Contracts & Legal, Redwood Inference
laura_bennett@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Initial SLA ask and latency carve-in for batch workloads

Quick engineering note — thanks for the context. A few practical points to set expectations:

- Interactive latency: for committed Dedicated pools we can consistently hit p95 ~180–220ms depending on model size and sequence length. p99 will vary with tail events (cache cold starts, VM preemption, network blips). Setting p99 < 600ms is achievable for most small-to-medium transformer models.
- Batched windows: batch jobs are often IO- or GPU-bound and can produce high tail latency spikes. We typically isolate these to dedicated job queues; if Nimbus can commit to explicit batch windows (e.g., daily 02:00–06:00 PT), we can exclude those windows from interactive SLOs and map them to a separate remedy schedule.
- Measurement: recommend instrumenting with our tracing hooks (request IDs + route labels) and agreeing to a monthly sample set for SLA evaluation. That avoids disputes on incident classification.

If Nimbus wants the tighter 99.95% baseline on Hosted without Dedicated, we'd need a formal capacity reservation during peak windows (and an associated uplifted commitment).

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Engineer, Inference Runtime, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial SLA ask and latency carve-in for batch workloads — proposed compromise and next steps

Hi Alice — thanks for the quick back-and-forth and the helpful redlines. To summarize the proposed path (so legal and procurement have a single reference):

1) Baselines
- Hosted (self-serve API): 99.90% uptime baseline. Monthly remedy table capped at 10% of monthly invoice.
- Dedicated (12‑month committed capacity): 99.92% baseline, with a one-time uplift clause that can reach 99.95% after a measured 90‑day stability period and defined commit level.

2) Monthly remedy and caps
- Remedy tiers will follow Redwood's standard table (tiered percentage based on monthly uptime bands). Top cap set at 10% unless Nimbus provides a written financial rationale to move higher.

3) Latency SLOs and carveouts
- Interactive SLO (Dedicated): p95 < 250ms, p99 < 750ms (as documented).
- Batched inference carveout: exclude defined batch windows (Nimbus to provide schedule) and place batch jobs on a separate remedy table. Batch windows will be explicitly described in Exhibit X.
- Measurement: use request-level tracing and monthly sample sets; incidents to be classified per incident playbook (shared link).

4) Maintenance and notification
- Scheduled maintenance: 7-day notice for non-urgent, 24-hour notice for minor updates, immediate for critical security fixes. Emergency maintenance still carved out but requires post-event report.

Next steps:
- Alice / Procurement: confirm whether Nimbus can accept the 10% remedy cap or propose an alternate cap and send final batch-window schedule by EOD Friday.
- Laura / Legal: will draft the contract exhibit reflecting the above and produce a DocuSign envelope for signature.
- Karthik / Eng: prepare the tracing guide and sample queries for Nimbus to instrument.

I'll attach a consolidated offer (final_sla_offer_v3.pdf) and a DocuSign link to accelerate when you're ready. If Nimbus signs the Dedicated 12‑month commit, we can start provisioning a reserved pool and schedule a stabilization trial.

Thanks — happy to hop on a short call if you want to walk this.

Best,
Priyom
